title: One Follicle Wins, Then Estradiol Flips

scenes.tts: A crowd of small follicles starts to grow. A follicle is an oocyte with the cells around it. Yet one oocyte is released, at a predictable time after a hormone surge. How does the ovary turn a crowd into one? First, F S H picks one follicle. Then that follicle's estradiol turns a brake into an accelerator.

scenes.tts: At the end of the previous cycle, F S H rises. It rescues a cohort of small antral follicles from atresia, the degeneration that ends almost every follicle. The rescued follicles make inhibin B, then mostly estradiol. Each suppresses pituitary F S H. The cohort lowers the very hormone that saved it. As F S H falls, usually just one follicle keeps growing; L H receptors help. It becomes dominant. The rest undergo atresia.
scenes.visual: FSH curve rises then falls; follicle thresholds as dashed lines; follicles drop out one by one as FSH falls below each threshold; one stays and is marked dominant

scenes.tts: In the human follicle before ovulation, two cell types share the work. Theca cells, outside the basement membrane, carry L H receptors and an enzyme, C Y P seventeen. They make androgen. Granulosa cells, inside, carry F S H receptors and aromatase, which converts the androgen to estrogen. As granulosa cells mature under F S H, they gain L H receptors. In the model, the most mature follicle can respond to L H while F S H falls.
scenes.visual: follicle wall as two stacked blocks across a basement membrane bar: theca outside with LH receptor and CYP17, granulosa inside with FSH receptor and aromatase; androgen arrow crosses, estrogen leaves; granulosa gains LH receptor
scenes.caption: In the human follicle before ovulation, two cell types share the work. Theca cells, outside the basement membrane, carry LH receptors and an enzyme, CYP17. They make androgen. Granulosa cells, inside, carry FSH receptors and aromatase, which converts the androgen to estrogen. As granulosa cells mature under FSH, they gain LH receptors. In the model, the most mature follicle can respond to LH while FSH falls.

scenes.tts: For most of the cycle, estradiol is a brake. It lowers G N R H release and L H release. Late in the follicular phase, the sign reverses. When estradiol from the dominant follicle stays high for long enough, it becomes positive feedback, and L H climbs steeply in the L H surge. Most mechanistic work is in mice, so human circuitry is less certain.

scenes.tts: In this sketch, F S H rises at the end of the previous cycle and falls through the mid-follicular phase. Estradiol climbs to a late-follicular peak. L H surges within a day of that peak. Textbooks place surge onset roughly thirty-four to thirty-six hours before ovulation, and intervals vary widely. Progesterone begins to rise shortly before the surge and climbs after ovulation, with a second, smaller rise of estradiol. At the cycle's end, F S H rises again.

scenes.tts: After ovulation, the corpus luteum secretes progesterone. In a 1984 study, blood was drawn every ten minutes for twenty-four hours from normally cycling women. In the mid and late luteal phase, progesterone rose in episodes after L H pulses. Across the sampled women and times, values ranged from two point three to forty point one nanograms per millilitre. One sample cannot measure a day of luteal output. Read a pulsatile hormone as a sequence in time, not from one sample.
scenes.visual: progesterone episodic trace beneath LH pulses with sample points every 10 min; range bracket 2.3 to 40.1 ng/mL; single sample marker
scenes.caption: After ovulation, the corpus luteum secretes progesterone. In a 1984 study, blood was drawn every 10 minutes for 24 hours from normally cycling women. In the mid and late luteal phase, progesterone rose in episodes after LH pulses. Across the sampled women and times, values ranged from 2.3 to 40.1 ng per mL. One sample cannot measure a day of luteal output. Read a pulsatile hormone as a sequence in time, not from one sample.
